Pay attention to word combinations. **Assistir** meaning “watch” normally uses **a**:

**Ontem, assisti ao filme com a minha irmã.** Yesterday, I watched the film with my sister.

For “help”, use **ajudar**:

**Ajudei o empregado de mesa a levar as chávenas.** I helped the waiter carry the cups.

For “eventually”, use **finalmente** when you mean “in the end”:

**Finalmente, encontrei as chaves no bolso do casaco.** Eventually, I found the keys in my coat.

For “actual” meaning “real”, use **real**, **verdadeiro** or **de facto**, depending on the sentence:

**O problema real é a falta de tempo.** The actual problem is the lack of time.

A small spelling difference can also change the meaning:

**Guardei o documento numa pasta do computador.** I saved the document in a computer folder.  
**Comi massa ao almoço.** I ate pasta for lunch.

## Erros comuns

1. **Using “pretender” for “to pretend”**

In Portuguese, **pretender** means “to intend” or “to plan”. For “to pretend”, use **fingir**.

**Ela pretende mudar de emprego.** She intends to change jobs.  
**Ele fingiu que não me viu.** He pretended that he did not see me.

2. **Using “eventualmente” for “eventually”**

**Eventualmente** usually means “possibly” or “occasionally”, not “in the end”.

**Eventualmente, podemos apanhar o autocarro.** We can possibly take the bus.  
**Finalmente, chegámos a casa.** Eventually, we arrived home.

3. **Translating “embarrassed” as “embaraçado”**

For a person who feels embarrassed, use **envergonhado** or **constrangido**. **Embaraçado** can mean tangled or awkward.

**Fiquei envergonhada quando me esqueci do nome dele.** I felt embarrassed when I forgot his name.  
**O fio ficou embaraçado no bolso.** The wire got tangled in the pocket.

title: The Personal Infinitive
blurbEn: You'll be able to say whose action you mean in sentences where English simply leaves it vague.
notePrompt: Teach the personal infinitive as the answer to one question: whose action is it? Contrast 'É difícil sair' (in general) with 'É difícil sairmos' (difficult for us to leave), and 'É melhor esperar' with 'É melhor esperarem'. Show the endings as the plain infinitive plus -, -es, -, -mos, -em, and note that this structure has no English equivalent at all, which is exactly why English speakers avoid it — either flattening everything to the impersonal infinitive or reaching for a 'que' clause with the subjunctive they have not learnt yet. Sell it as the thing that lets them say complex sentences a whole level early.
noteMd:
## O que é

The personal infinitive is a special form of the infinitive that shows who is doing the action. English usually uses a subject with a finite verb, or sometimes “for + person + to”:

**É importante estudarmos todos os dias.** It is important for us to study every day.

**Antes de saíres, fecha a janela.** Before you leave, close the window.

**Depois de eles chegarem, começamos a reunião.** After they arrive, we will start the meeting.

Unlike the ordinary, impersonal infinitive, the personal infinitive changes according to the subject. It is especially useful when the subject of the infinitive is different from the subject of the main verb, or when you want to make the subject very clear.

**É melhor ficares em casa hoje.** It is better for you to stay at home today.

Here, *ficares* tells us that “you” should stay, not necessarily the person speaking.

## Como funciona

The personal infinitive uses the ordinary infinitive plus endings for most persons. The first-person singular and third-person singular have no special ending, so the context tells us who the subject is.

Using **falar** as an example:

| Person | Form | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| eu | **falar** | for me to speak |
| tu | **falares** | for you to speak |
| ele/ela | **falar** | for him/her to speak |
| nós | **falarmos** | for us to speak |
| vós | **falardes** | for you plural to speak; uncommon in everyday speech |
| eles/elas | **falarem** | for them to speak |

The same endings are used with **comer** and **partir**:

**É importante comermos antes da viagem.** It is important for us to eat before the journey.

**Sem partires agora, ainda chegas a horas.** If you do not leave now, you will still arrive on time.

The personal infinitive commonly appears after prepositions such as **antes de**, **depois de**, **sem**, **por** and **para**. Use it when the subject needs to be stated or is different from the main subject.

**Depois de terminares o trabalho, podes descansar.** After you finish the work, you can rest.

**Saímos sem eles saberem.** We left without them knowing.

It can also follow expressions such as **é importante**, **é melhor**, **é difícil** and **é possível**:

**É possível encontrarmos uma solução.** It is possible for us to find a solution.

If the subject is clearly the same as the main subject, the ordinary infinitive is often enough:

**Depois de comer, lavei os dentes.** After eating, I brushed my teeth.

If you want to show that someone else ate, use the personal infinitive:

**Depois de o meu irmão comer, lavei os dentes.** After my brother ate, I brushed my teeth.

Do not confuse the personal infinitive with the future subjunctive. After **antes de**, use the infinitive; after **quando**, use the future subjunctive:

**Antes de chegarmos, telefona-me.** Before we arrive, call me.

**Quando chegarmos, telefona-me.** When we arrive, call me.

## Erros comuns

1. **Using the English-style “for + person + to” structure**

English speakers may try to translate directly:

**É importante para nós estudar.** It is important for us to study.

This is possible in some contexts, but the more natural structure here is:

**É importante estudarmos.** It is important for us to study.

2. **Forgetting the personal ending**

Do not use the ordinary infinitive when the subject is clearly **tu**, **nós** or **eles**:

**Antes de tu sair, avisa-me.** Before you leave, let me know.

The correct form is:

**Antes de saíres, avisa-me.** Before you leave, let me know.

Similarly:

**É melhor irmos de autocarro.** It is better for us to go by bus.

3. **Using the personal infinitive after “quando”**

The personal infinitive does not normally follow **quando** for a future event:

**Quando chegarmos, começamos.** When we arrive, we will start.

Not:

**Quando chegarmos?** when you mean “before arriving”. Use **antes de chegarmos** for that meaning. Portuguese has several forms for “when”, “before” and “after”; naturally, it would be too simple otherwise.

title: The Personal Infinitive After Prepositions
titlePt: O Infinitivo Pessoal Regido por Preposição
blurbEn: You'll be able to use the frames Portuguese people use every day — antes de saírem, para não teres de esperar, apesar de estarmos atrasados.
notePrompt: Drill the high-frequency frames: 'antes de', 'depois de', 'para', 'até', 'sem', 'apesar de', 'no caso de' and 'por' plus a personal infinitive whose ending names the doer — 'Liguei antes de saírem', 'Deixei a chave para não teres de esperar', 'Saímos sem eles darem por nada'. Contrast each with the English -ing clause the learner is translating from ('before they left', 'without them noticing') and forbid the gerund outright: 'sem eles perceberem', never 'sem eles percebendo'. Push the learner to notice that a single ending is doing the work of a whole subject clause.
noteMd:
## O que é

This unit explains how to use the **personal infinitive** after a preposition. In European Portuguese, the infinitive can show who does the action. This is especially useful when the subject is different from the subject of the main verb, or when we want to make the subject very clear.

Compare these sentences:

**Saí sem comer.** I left without eating.  
The person who left and the person who ate are the same: *I*.

**Saí sem eles comerem.** I left without them eating.  
The subject of *comerem* is different: *eles*.

**É importante estudarmos antes do exame.** It is important for us to study before the exam.  
Here, the ending **-armos** tells us that *we* are the people who study.

The personal infinitive is not a completely different tense. It is the infinitive with a personal ending. Portuguese, naturally, decided that one infinitive was not quite enough.

## Como funciona

The personal infinitive is commonly used after prepositions such as **para**, **sem**, **antes de**, **depois de**, **por**, and **ao**. Use it when the subject is expressed or when the subject is different from the main clause.

For regular verbs ending in **-ar**, the pattern is:

| Subject | *falar* |
|---|---|
| eu | **falar** — for me to speak |
| tu | **falares** — for you to speak |
| ele/ela | **falar** — for him/her to speak |
| nós | **falarmos** — for us to speak |
| eles/elas | **falarem** — for them to speak |

The **eu** and **ele/ela** forms look the same. The subject, or the context, tells us who is doing the action.

With **para**, use the personal infinitive when the subject is clear and expressed:

**Trouxe os documentos para tu assinares.** I brought the documents for you to sign.  
**Trouxe os documentos para eu assinar.** I brought the documents for me to sign.

Do not use **mim** as the subject of the infinitive. *Mim* is an object form, so say **para eu fazer**, not *para mim fazer*.

With **sem**, **antes de**, and **depois de**, the same idea applies:

**Ela saiu sem nós repararmos.** She left without us noticing.  
**Lava as mãos antes de começares a cozinhar.** Wash your hands before you start cooking.  
**Depois de chegarmos, telefonámos aos nossos amigos.** After we arrived, we phoned our friends.

The infinitive also appears after **ao**, usually with a meaning like “when” or “on” doing something:

**Ao entrares, fecha a porta, por favor.** When you come in, close the door, please.  
**Ao chegarem a casa, encontraram uma mensagem.** When they arrived home, they found a message.

If the subject is the same and there is no need to emphasise it, the ordinary infinitive is often enough:

**Fui ao mercado para comprar fruta.** I went to the market to buy fruit.  
The implied subject of both verbs is *eu*, so the simple infinitive works perfectly.

## Erros comuns

1. **Using a subject pronoun as an object**

English speakers may translate “for me to…” as *para mim fazer*. In Portuguese, the person doing the action is the subject, so use **eu**:

**Isto é para eu levar.** This is for me to take.  
Not *Isto é para mim levar.*

2. **Using the wrong personal ending**

Remember that the ending must match the subject:

**É melhor vocês esperarem aqui.** It is better for you to wait here.  
Not *É melhor vocês esperar aqui.*

With **tu**, use **-res**; with **nós**, use **-rmos**; with **eles/elas**, use **-rem**:

**É importante tu leres as instruções.** It is important for you to read the instructions.

3. **Using the personal infinitive when the subject is unnecessary**

Do not add an ending automatically. When the subject is the same and already obvious, the simple infinitive is natural:

**Fiquei em casa para descansar.** I stayed at home to rest.  
Not usually *para eu descansar* — although that form is possible when you want extra contrast or emphasis.

title: The Doctor and the Centro de Saúde
titlePt: No Centro de Saúde e no Médico
blurbEn: You'll be able to book an appointment, describe a symptom accurately, and follow what the doctor tells you to do next.
notePrompt: Teach the whole path: 'marcar uma consulta', 'o médico de família', 'o número de utente', 'a urgência', 'a triagem de Manchester' and its colours, 'a receita sem papel', 'as análises', 'a baixa'. Drill symptoms with 'doer' as an indirect construction — 'dói-me a cabeça', 'doem-me as costas' — because the thing that hurts is the subject and the person is the clitic; English speakers say 'eu tenho dor de' or try to conjugate 'doer' for themselves. Also contrast 'estou constipado' (a head cold) with 'estou entupido', and note that 'sinto-me maldisposto' means queasy, not badly dressed.
noteMd:
## O que é

This unit is for talking about visits to the **centro de saúde**, describing symptoms, making an appointment and understanding a doctor’s advice. You will practise explaining how you feel, how long you have had a problem and what you need to do next.

**Queria marcar uma consulta porque não me sinto bem há dois dias.** I would like to make an appointment because I have not been feeling well for two days.

**Estou a sentir uma dor forte no peito e tenho dificuldade em respirar.** I am feeling a strong pain in my chest and I am having difficulty breathing.

**A médica disse-me para descansar e beber muita água.** The doctor told me to rest and drink plenty of water.

At B1 level, it is useful to give precise information: when the symptoms started, whether they are getting better or worse, and what you have already taken. Portuguese, naturally, has several ways to say that something hurts. It likes to keep us alert.

## Como funciona

To describe symptoms, use **ter**, **sentir** and **doer**:

| Structure | Example |
|---|---|
| **ter + noun** | **Tenho febre e tosse.** I have a fever and a cough. |
| **sentir + noun** | **Sinto uma pressão no peito.** I feel pressure in my chest. |
| **doer + pronoun** | **Dói-me a cabeça.** My head hurts. |

With **doer**, the body part is grammatically the subject, while **me/te/lhe** shows who feels the pain. Compare:

**Dói-me o estômago.** My stomach hurts.  
**Dói-lhe a garganta.** His/her throat hurts.  
**Doem-me as costas.** My back hurts.

For an ongoing symptom, use **estar a + infinitive**, not the gerund:

**Estou a tossir desde ontem.** I have been coughing since yesterday.  
**A febre está a baixar.** The fever is going down.

To say how long something has continued, use **há** with the present tense:

**Tenho dores nas costas há uma semana.** I have had back pain for a week.

When speaking to a doctor or nurse, you will often need object pronouns. In a plain affirmative sentence, they come after the verb and join it with a hyphen:

**Vou marcar a consulta amanhã.** I am going to book the appointment tomorrow.  
**Vou marcá-la amanhã.** I am going to book it tomorrow.  
**A enfermeira chamou-me.** The nurse called me.  
**O médico explicou-me o tratamento.** The doctor explained the treatment to me.

After a negative word or a question word, the pronoun normally comes before the verb:

**Não me sinto melhor.** I do not feel better.  
**Quando te começaram os sintomas?** When did your symptoms start?  
**O que lhe dói?** What hurts?

Useful vocabulary includes **a consulta** (appointment/consultation), **a receita** (prescription), **as análises** (tests), **a baixa médica** (sick note), **os sintomas**, **a febre**, **a tosse**, **as tonturas** and **a dor**.

## Erros comuns

1. English speakers often translate “I am feeling” with a gerund. In European Portuguese, say:

**Estou a sentir-me muito cansado.** I am feeling very tired.

Not *estou a sentir-me*. The structure is **estar a + infinitive**.

2. Do not put the object pronoun before the verb in a plain affirmative sentence:

**Diga-me o que aconteceu.** Tell me what happened.  
**Levei-lhe os resultados das análises.** I took him/her the test results.

Not *me diga* or *lhe levei* in these plain affirmative sentences. After **não**, however, it moves before the verb:

**Não me diga isso.** Do not tell me that.

3. English speakers may use a subject pronoun instead of an object pronoun:

**Vi-o na sala de espera.** I saw him in the waiting room.  
**Encontrei-a no centro de saúde.** I found her at the health centre.

Not *vi ele* or *encontrei ela* in careful European Portuguese.

title: Buying a House
blurbEn: You'll be able to follow a viewing, understand the offer-to-deed sequence, and ask a solicitor the questions that actually matter.
notePrompt: Walk the sequence in Portuguese terms: 'a visita', 'a proposta', 'o CPCV (contrato-promessa de compra e venda)', 'o sinal', 'a escritura', 'o notário', 'a caderneta predial', 'a certidão permanente', 'a licença de utilização', 'o IMT e o imposto do selo', 'o IMI anual'. Contrast 'o sinal' with an English deposit — it is forfeited if the buyer walks and doubled back if the seller does — and contrast 'a caderneta predial' (the tax record of a property) with the school caderneta. English speakers say 'depósito' for 'sinal' and 'contrato' for 'CPCV', which makes an estate agent believe a different stage has been reached.
noteMd:
## O que é

This unit helps you talk about buying a property in Portugal: describing a house, asking an estate agent questions, discussing money and documents, and making an offer. At B1 level, you should be able to explain what you are looking for and understand the main stages of the process.

**Estou à procura de uma casa com dois quartos e uma varanda.** I am looking for a house with two bedrooms and a balcony.

**Gostaria de saber se o preço inclui o lugar de estacionamento.** I would like to know whether the price includes the parking space.

**A casa parece interessante, mas preciso de confirmar algumas informações antes de fazer uma proposta.** The house seems interesting, but I need to confirm some information before making an offer.

Buying property involves quite a lot of specific vocabulary. Portuguese bureaucracy also likes documents with long names. It is best to learn the important terms as complete expressions, rather than translating each word separately.

## Como funciona

When viewing a property, use **procuro** or **estou à procura de** to say what you want. Use **tem** to ask whether something exists, and **fica** to ask about location.

**A casa fica perto do mercado e do autocarro?** Is the house near the market and the bus?

**O prédio tem elevador?** Does the building have a lift?

**Há obras para fazer?** Is there work to be done?

Some useful property vocabulary:

| Portuguese | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **a moradia** | detached or semi-detached house |
| **o apartamento / o andar** | flat / apartment |
| **o rés-do-chão** | ground floor |
| **o primeiro andar** | first floor |
| **a área útil** | usable floor area |
| **o lugar de estacionamento** | parking space |
| **o condomínio** | building management and shared costs |
| **a prestação** | regular mortgage payment |
| **a entrada** | deposit or initial payment |
| **o crédito à habitação** | mortgage |
| **a escritura** | the final property deed |

Three documents and agreements are especially useful to recognise:

- **a caderneta predial**: a tax document describing the property;
- **a licença de utilização**: confirmation that the property can be used legally;
- **o contrato-promessa de compra e venda (CPCV)**: a preliminary agreement made before the final deed.

A common sequence is:

**Primeiro, visitamos a casa. Depois, fazemos uma proposta e negociamos o preço.** First, we visit the house. Then, we make an offer and negotiate the price.

**Se o proprietário aceitar a proposta, assinamos o contrato-promessa e pagamos o sinal.** If the owner accepts the offer, we sign the preliminary contract and pay the deposit.

For polite questions, **gostaria de saber se…** is very useful. In a plain affirmative sentence, object pronouns normally come after the verb, joined by a hyphen:

**Pode mostrar-me a caderneta predial?** Can you show me the property tax document?

**O agente enviou-me os documentos por e-mail.** The agent sent me the documents by email.

After a negative word, the pronoun comes before the verb:

**Ainda não me enviaram o contrato.** They have not sent me the contract yet.

## Erros comuns

1. **Translating “I want” too directly**

In a property search, **quero** can sound rather blunt, especially with an estate agent. **Gostaria de…** is more polite and natural.

**Gostaria de marcar uma visita à casa.** I would like to arrange a viewing of the house.

2. **Confusing “preço”, “prestação” and “sinal”**

The **preço** is the total price. The **prestação** is a regular mortgage payment. The **sinal** is money paid when signing the preliminary agreement.

**Qual é o preço total e qual seria a prestação mensal?** What is the total price and what would the monthly payment be?

3. **Using the wrong pronoun position**

Do not say *me diga* in a plain affirmative request. In European Portuguese, say:

**Diga-me se a casa tem licença de utilização.** Tell me whether the house has a use licence.

But after **não**, the pronoun moves before the verb:

**Não me diga que ainda falta outro documento!** Don’t tell me that another document is still missing!

title: Compound Adjectives
blurbEn: You'll be able to describe things with the two-part adjectives Portuguese uses constantly — recém-chegado, mal-humorado, luso-britânico, verde-escuro.
notePrompt: Teach the agreement rule that surprises everyone: in a compound adjective only the final element agrees ('uma família luso-britânica', 'olhos verde-escuros'), and a colour compound containing a noun is invariable ('camisas verde-garrafa', 'olhos cor de mel'). Cover the productive prefixes recém-, mal-, bem-, meio-, semi- and the hyphen after the 1990 spelling agreement. The English-speaker error is making both halves agree, as in 'camisas escuras verdes' or 'uma família lusa-britânica' — show the wrong and right forms side by side.

title: Object Pronouns: Third Person
titlePt: Os Pronomes Clíticos de Terceira Pessoa: o, a, os, as
blurbEn: You'll be able to say 'I saw him', 'I bought it' and 'I told her' without repeating the whole noun every single time.
notePrompt: Teach the two columns separately: direct o/a/os/as ('Vi-o ontem') and indirect lhe/lhes ('Falei-lhe ontem'). Contrast them by verb, because Portuguese decides which column a verb takes and it does not match English intuition — 'telefonar a alguém' and 'responder a alguém' take lhe, while 'ver' and 'ajudar' take o/a. Drill the enclitic hyphen as the default in a plain affirmative sentence, then the proclitic shift after 'não', 'já', 'que', 'quem', 'todos', 'nunca' and 'só' ('não o vi'). The English-speaker error is putting the pronoun before the verb everywhere, Brazilian-style: 'eu o vi'.

title: Object Pronouns: -lo, -la and the Merged Forms
titlePt: Clíticos: -lo, -la e as Formas Contraídas (lho, lha)
blurbEn: You'll be able to read and say 'vou comprá-lo' and 'dei-lha' — the two shapes that make written Portuguese unreadable until you've met them.
notePrompt: Teach two mechanical rules. First: after a verb form ending in -r, -s or -z that ending drops and o/a/os/as becomes -lo/-la/-los/-las, with an accent surfacing on the stressed vowel — 'comprar + o' gives 'comprá-lo', 'fazer + o' gives 'fazê-lo', 'pôr + as' gives 'pô-las', 'fizemos + o' gives 'fizemo-lo'. Second: an indirect and a direct pronoun merge — me + o = mo, te + a = ta, lhe + a = lha, lhes + os = lhos ('Dei-lha ontem'). Add -no/-na after a nasal ('dão-no'). English speakers read 'comprá-lo' as an unknown word and never produce 'lha' at all, saying 'dei ela a ele' or the Brazilian 'dei para ela' — name that workaround and replace it.

title: Driving: The IMT and Your Licence
titlePt: Conduzir: O IMT e a Carta de Condução
blurbEn: You'll be able to exchange a foreign licence at the IMT, register a car, and understand exactly which document you're being asked for.
notePrompt: Cover the counter and the paperwork: 'trocar a carta de condução', 'o atestado médico', 'o registo automóvel', 'o DUA (documento único automóvel)', 'o livrete' as the old word people still use, 'a matrícula', 'o seguro contra terceiros', 'o IUC'. Flag the acronym collision head-on: the IMT you visit is the Instituto da Mobilidade e dos Transportes, while the IMT you pay when buying a house is the Imposto Municipal sobre as Transmissões. Also note 'a matrícula' means both number plate and school enrolment. The English-speaker error is 'a licença de condução', a calque nobody uses — in Portugal it is simply 'a carta'.

title: On the Road: Inspection, Tolls and the GNR
titlePt: Na Estrada: A Inspeção, as Portagens e a GNR
blurbEn: You'll be able to book and pass the IPO inspection, deal with tolls, and handle being waved down by the GNR without panicking.
notePrompt: Build the roadside encounter as listening first: 'Documentos, faça favor', 'A carta e os documentos do carro', 'Sabe a que velocidade seguia?', 'Sopre aqui', 'Pode seguir'. Then the rest: 'a inspeção periódica obrigatória (IPO)', 'reprovou na inspeção', 'a Via Verde', 'as portagens', 'a multa', 'o limite de velocidade', 'a berma', 'o pisca'. Contrast GNR (roads and rural areas) with PSP (inside cities) so the learner knows who has stopped them. English speakers freeze because the officer uses formal third person with no pronoun at all — 'Tem a carta consigo?' — so train that exact shape, tying it back to the formal register unit.

title: School: The Caderneta and Talking to Teachers
titlePt: Na Escola: A Caderneta e as Reuniões de Pais
blurbEn: You'll be able to read a note that comes home in the caderneta, hold a parent-teacher meeting, and understand how Portuguese school years and grades actually work.
notePrompt: Teach the system and its paperwork together: 'a caderneta do aluno', 'o diretor de turma', 'a reunião de pais', 'a matrícula', 'o 9.º ano', 'o ensino básico e o secundário', 'os exames nacionais', 'a equivalência de habilitações', 'a falta justificada', 'a avaliação'. Contrast the Portuguese 0-20 marking scale with A-F so a parent does not read a 14 as a failure, and contrast 'a nota' (a mark) with 'o recado' (the message a teacher writes home). English-speaking parents write a textbook 'Prezado professor' letter — teach instead that a caderneta reply is short and signed: 'Tomei conhecimento' plus the encarregado de educação's signature.

title: Past Participles
blurbEn: You'll be able to read the participles that fill every sign, contract and notice — fechado, proibido, entregue — and use them to describe states and say what was done.
notePrompt: Teach the participle as an adjective that agrees ('a porta está fechada', 'os documentos foram entregues'), then build the passive: ser for the action ('a casa foi vendida em maio') against estar for the resulting state ('a casa está vendida'). Give the irregulars that earn their keep — feito, dito, visto, posto, aberto, escrito, ganho, pago, gasto, vindo — and the double forms, noting that Portugal prefers 'entregue' and 'aceite' over 'entregado' and 'aceitado'. Do not introduce compound tenses here. The English-speaker error is leaving the participle invariable as in English: 'as cartas foram enviado'.

title: Work and Employment
blurbEn: You'll be able to describe what you do for a living, read a job advert, and make sense of a Portuguese payslip and contract.
notePrompt: Cover both halves: talking about work ('trabalho por conta própria', 'passo recibos verdes', 'trabalho a partir de casa', 'estou reformado') and the paperwork ('o contrato sem termo', 'o período experimental', 'o recibo de vencimento', 'o subsídio de férias e o de Natal', 'a Segurança Social', 'as horas extraordinárias', 'o salário mínimo'). Contrast 'o emprego' (a specific post) with 'o trabalho' (work in general), and 'a reforma' (retirement, a pension) with the English reform. Two errors to fix: the gerund in 'estou trabalhando' — it is 'estou a trabalhar' — and the article in 'sou um professor', since professions drop it: 'sou professor'.

title: A Tour of Portugal: Regions, Art and Culture
titlePt: Uma Volta por Portugal: Regiões, Arte e Cultura
blurbEn: You'll be able to talk about where you've been and what each part of the country is known for, and hold your own when the conversation turns to fado, azulejos or a saint's day.
notePrompt: Move north to south — Minho, Douro, Beiras, Estremadura e Oeste, Ribatejo, Alentejo, Algarve, Açores e Madeira — with one dish, one landscape and one cultural anchor each; then the shared culture: o fado, os azulejos, a calçada portuguesa, Camões e Pessoa, os Santos Populares, as festas e os feriados. Contrast the tourist Portugal an expat arrives with (Lisboa e o Algarve) against the country their neighbours actually talk about. Drill the place prepositions English speakers get wrong: 'em Lisboa' but 'no Porto', 'no Alentejo' but 'na Madeira', and 'ir a' (go and come back) against 'ir para' (go and stay).

title: The Oeste: The Market, the Wine and Carnaval de Torres
titlePt: O Oeste: A Feira, o Vinho e o Carnaval de Torres
blurbEn: You'll be able to shop the weekly feira in Torres Vedras, talk about the wine the Oeste actually grows, and know what's happening when the whole town shuts down for Carnaval.
notePrompt: Ground everything in the family's own region. The weekly feira in Torres Vedras and the market at Santa Cruz: 'meio quilo', 'um molho de couves', 'é da terra?', 'quanto é ao todo?', 'leve mais um que eu arredondo'. The Oeste as a wine region: 'a vinha', 'a adega', 'a vindima', 'o vinho da região', 'a aguardente da Lourinhã'. Carnaval de Torres: 'as matrafonas', 'os cabeçudos', 'os carros alegóricos', 'os Zés Pereiras', 'o corso'. Contrast 'a feira' (the weekly open-air market) with 'o mercado' (the covered municipal building), and 'o talho', 'a peixaria' and 'a padaria' with a supermarket aisle. The error to fix is buying by unit — 'dois tomates' earns a strange look where 'meio quilo de tomate' does not.

title: Reported Speech
blurbEn: You'll be able to tell your family what the clerk, the doctor or the diretora de turma actually said, instead of shrugging.
notePrompt: Teach the backshift as a small set of swaps: presente to imperfeito ('Está fechado' becomes 'Disse que estava fechado'), futuro to condicional ('Virá amanhã' becomes 'Disse que viria no dia seguinte'), and the pretérito perfeito left as it is in speech, since the compound pluperfect belongs to a later level. Add the pronoun, possessive and time shifts: hoje to nesse dia, amanhã to no dia seguinte, aqui to ali. Drill 'perguntar se' for yes/no questions ('Perguntou se eu tinha o NIF') and 'pedir para' plus infinitive for requests ('Pediu para eu voltar na quinta'). The English-speaker errors are keeping the original tense — 'Ele disse que está fechado', which reads as a live quote — and using 'que' after 'perguntar' where Portuguese needs 'se'. Use no subjunctive.

title: Listening to the Oeste Accent
blurbEn: You'll be able to understand your actual neighbours — the Estremadura and Oeste speech that no course records and that defeats you at the talho counter.
notePrompt: Train comprehension on real regional features rather than studio Portuguese: vowel reduction pushed to disappearance ('está bem' to 'tá bem' to something near 'tâim'), swallowed final syllables, 'p'ra' for 'para', 'tou' for 'estou', 'num' for 'não', 'ó' for 'olha', 'pá' as a filler, and the very closed 'e' of rural Estremadura. Contrast the Lisbon-standard audio the learner has trained on with an older speaker from Torres Vedras or Santa Cruz saying the identical sentence. Address the false conclusion English speakers draw — that they need more vocabulary — when the real gap is that the words they know are stored unreduced; teach 'Desculpe, importa-se de repetir mais devagar?' and train prediction from context.

title: Society and Living Together
blurbEn: You'll be able to handle a condomínio meeting, a noise complaint and a favour from a neighbour without either escalating or caving in.
notePrompt: Teach the lexicon and etiquette of shared life in a Portuguese town — condomínio, quota, administrador (never the pt-BR 'síndico'), assembleia de condóminos, junta de freguesia, vizinho do lado, dar-se bem com, fazer um favor, ficar mal visto — plus the pt-PT preference for impersonal, question-shaped complaints; the anchor contrast is the direct English 'You're being too loud' against 'Se calhar não dava para baixar um bocadinho?', and the classic English-speaker error is the bare tu imperative ('Baixa o som') where Portuguese hedges, plus reading 'convivência' as cold 'coexistence' when it carries the warmer sense of getting on with people.
noteMd:
## O que é

In shared life, the goal is not simply to say what is wrong. It is to protect the relationship while still asking for something practical: less noise, a payment, a repair, a favour or a decision at a meeting. In European Portuguese, complaints between neighbours are often softened by making them sound less like an accusation and more like a possible solution.

Listen to these everyday examples:

**Se calhar não dava para baixar um bocadinho o som?** — Perhaps you could turn the sound down a little?

**Será que podiam evitar arrastar as cadeiras depois das dez?** — Could you avoid dragging the chairs after ten?

**Não te importavas de me fazer um favor e receber uma encomenda amanhã?** — Would you mind doing me a favour and receiving a parcel tomorrow?

All three are direct enough to be useful, but they leave the other person room to cooperate without losing face. That is central to **a convivência**: not cold “coexistence”, but the warmer idea of getting on with the people around you and sharing space well.

## Como funciona

The most useful pattern for a complaint is an impersonal, question-shaped sentence:

- **Será que dava para + infinitive?** — Would it be possible to…?
- **Não dava para + infinitive?** — Couldn’t you…?
- **Se calhar não dava para + infinitive?** — Perhaps you could…?

The verb **dar** here means “to be possible”, not “to give”. The imperfect form **dava** makes the request less abrupt than a direct present-tense command. The subject is deliberately vague: instead of saying “you are causing a problem”, you ask whether a solution is possible.

**Será que dava para falarem um pouco mais baixo?** — Would it be possible for you to speak a little more quietly?

**Se calhar não dava para estacionares um pouco mais à frente?** — Perhaps you could park a little further ahead?

With **tu**, use the infinitive after **para**: **para baixares**, **para estacionares**, **para avisares**. With several people or a formal group, use **podiam** and the plural infinitive structure:

**Será que podiam fechar a porta da entrada devagar?** — Could you close the entrance door quietly?

The bare **tu** imperative exists, but it is strong in a neighbour complaint:

**Baixa o som.** — Turn the sound down.

That may be perfectly normal between close friends or family, but with the **vizinho do lado** it can sound like an order. A softer version is usually safer.

For shared administration, these are worth memorising because they recur constantly:

| Portuguese | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **o condomínio** | the condominium / shared building |
| **a quota** | the regular condominium payment |
| **o administrador** | the building administrator |
| **a assembleia de condóminos** | the owners’ meeting |
| **a junta de freguesia** | the local civil parish council |

**O administrador marcou a assembleia de condóminos para quinta-feira.** — The administrator scheduled the owners’ meeting for Thursday.

**Ainda não pagaste a quota do condomínio?** — Haven’t you paid the condominium fee yet?

For social relationships, learn the whole expressions rather than translating word by word:

| Expression | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **dar-se bem com alguém** | to get on well with someone |
| **fazer um favor** | to do someone a favour |
| **ficar mal visto** | to be seen negatively / lose people’s respect |

**Damo-nos bem com os vizinhos, apesar de o prédio ser pequeno.** — We get on well with the neighbours, even though the building is small.

**Não quero ficar mal visto por estar sempre a reclamar.** — I don’t want to be seen negatively for always complaining.

## Na vida real

At a condominium meeting, be clear but collaborative:

**Acho que devíamos pedir um orçamento para arranjar a porta da garagem.** — I think we should ask for a quote to repair the garage door.

**Concordo, mas temos de ver se a quota chega para isso.** — I agree, but we need to see whether the condominium funds cover it.

If noise continues, add a fact and a reasonable request rather than a judgement:

**Desculpa incomodar, mas o barulho ouve-se bastante no nosso quarto. Será que podias baixar a música depois das dez?** — Sorry to bother you, but the noise can be heard quite clearly in our bedroom. Could you turn the music down after ten?

This works near Santa Cruz just as it does in a flat in Torres Vedras: mention the concrete effect, then ask for a manageable change. If the problem concerns rubbish, parking or a public space, the **junta de freguesia** may be the appropriate place to ask for help.

A favour also needs a little space for refusal:

**Se não te der jeito, não faz mal; posso pedir a outra pessoa.** — If it isn’t convenient for you, no problem; I can ask someone else.

That sentence prevents politeness from becoming pressure. The aim is neither to escalate nor to cave in.

## Erros comuns

1. **Directly translating “You’re being too loud”**

Wrong and very confrontational: **Estás a ser demasiado barulhento.** — You’re being too loud.

Better: **Se calhar não dava para baixares um bocadinho o som?** — Perhaps you could turn the sound down a little?

The direct version labels the person. The Portuguese version focuses on the action.

2. **Using a bare imperative with a neighbour**

Too blunt in this context: **Baixa o som.** — Turn the sound down.

Better: **Será que podias baixar um bocadinho o som?** — Could you turn the sound down a little?

The **tu** imperative is not grammatically wrong, but it is often socially too strong for a complaint.

3. **Using the wrong condominium word**

Avoid the Brazilian Portuguese term **síndico**. In pt-PT, say:

**Tenho de falar com o administrador do condomínio.** — I have to speak to the condominium administrator.

Also, **convivência** is not merely formal “coexistence”: **Boa convivência é importante entre vizinhos.** — Getting on well is important between neighbours.

title: Interjections and Discourse Markers
blurbEn: You'll be able to drop pois, epá, olha and então into your speech so you sound like you live here rather than like you're reciting sentences.
notePrompt: Teach the pt-PT particle set as meaning-carrying, not filler: pois (agreement or mild resignation) vs pois é vs the sarcastic pois sim, olha / olha lá as attention-getters, então? as both greeting and challenge, pronto as the wrap-up, epá as a neutral 'mate', and the deictic pair lá / cá (vou lá vs cá em casa, and 'eu cá acho que...' = 'personally I reckon'); the anchor contrast is that English speakers render 'well...' as 'bem' when pt-PT wants 'bom', 'então' or 'pronto', and they omit 'pois' entirely, which makes their agreement land as cold or grudging.

title: Diminutives and Augmentatives
blurbEn: You'll be able to use -inho and -ão to soften a request, warm up a thank-you, or land an insult on purpose rather than by accident.
notePrompt: Teach -inho/-zinho and -ão/-ona as register and affect rather than size: cafezinho (a coffee offered with warmth, not a small coffee), obrigadinho (affectionate or faintly sarcastic depending on tone), um bocadinho and daqui a bocadinho as politeness softeners, devagarinho, and the augmentative's split between admiration (mulherão) and abuse (palavrão, chorão); cover the attachment rule (café→cafezinho, mãe→mãezinha, casa→casinha) and address the English-speaker error of assuming the suffix always means 'small' and therefore avoiding it altogether, which makes every request sound curt — 'Dás-me um bocado de pão' vs 'Dás-me um bocadinho de pão'.

title: Idioms I: Body, Food and Animals
titlePt: Expressões Idiomáticas I: Corpo, Comida e Animais
blurbEn: You'll be able to follow the idioms that fly around a Portuguese family table instead of hearing a wall of literal nonsense.
notePrompt: Teach high-frequency pt-PT idioms grouped by source image — corpo (meter o pé na argola, estar com a pulga atrás da orelha, dar com a língua nos dentes, não ter papas na língua), comida (é canja, pão-pão queijo-queijo, ir com os porcos) and animais (ter macaquinhos no sótão, ver-se grego, estar à sombra da bananeira) — always giving the pragmatic force and the register, not just the gloss; the contrast to draw is idiom-for-idiom rather than word-for-word, and the English-speaker error is calquing ('it's a piece of cake' → *é um pedaço de bolo) instead of reaching for the Portuguese image that already exists, 'é canja'.

title: Idioms II: Work, Luck, the Sea and Proverbs
titlePt: Expressões Idiomáticas II: Trabalho, Sorte, Mar e Provérbios
blurbEn: You'll be able to close an argument with the same proverb your neighbour would reach for, and know when a proverb is the graceful way out.
notePrompt: Cover idioms of effort and fortune (dar o litro, andar numa roda-viva, ficar a ver navios, deitar água na fervura, estar com água pela barba, à espera que caia o maná) plus the provérbio as a conversational move — devagar se vai ao longe; quem não tem cão caça com gato; águas passadas não movem moinhos; grão a grão enche a galinha o papo; the contrast to draw is the English habit of quoting proverbs ironically or apologetically against the Portuguese habit of using one sincerely to end a disagreement without anyone losing face, and the error to correct is translating 'left high and dry' or 'up to my neck' literally when 'ficar a ver navios' and 'estar com água pela barba' already exist.

title: Slang and Street Portuguese
blurbEn: You'll be able to follow the teenagers and the café counter, and know which words you can say back and which you should only recognise.
notePrompt: Separate gíria (fixe, bué, ganda, cota, gajo/gaja, curtir, bazar, chunga, ter piada, estar-se nas tintas) from calão proper, and label every item produce-or-recognise-only, including which ones a parent can say in front of teenagers; the essential contrast is pt-PT fixe / bué / puto against pt-BR legal / muito / moleque, and the English-speaker error is importing Brazilian slang absorbed from music and streaming, which in the Oeste reads as either foreign or comic — also warn that 'gajo' is fine among friends and rude about a stranger, and that 'giro' means nice-looking, not funny.

title: Present Subjunctive
blurbEn: You'll be able to express doubt, desire, emotion and polite pressure — the whole 'I want you to...' family that Portuguese refuses to say with the indicative.
notePrompt: Build the presente do conjuntivo off the eu-form of the present indicative (faço→faça, tenho→tenha, digo→diga, ponho→ponha) with the six true irregulars (ser, estar, ir, haver, saber, querer), triggered by desire, doubt, emotion and impersonal judgement, and by para que, embora, talvez, antes que, sem que, a não ser que, caso; the anchor contrast is 'Quero que tu venhas' against the two English-speaker errors *'Quero que tu vens' and the infinitive calque *'Quero-te vir' straight from 'I want you to come' — English has no live morphological subjunctive, so the triggers must be learned as a list — and note that talvez takes the conjuntivo when it precedes the verb but the indicative when it follows ('Talvez venha' vs 'Ele vem, talvez').

title: Imperfect Subjunctive
blurbEn: You'll be able to say what you would do if things were different, and make requests so soft that refusing them politely is easy.
notePrompt: Derive the imperfeito do conjuntivo from the third person plural of the pretérito perfeito (fizeram→fizesse, foram→fosse, tiveram→tivesse, puderam→pudesse) so every irregular is inherited rather than memorised, then drill the fixed frame se + imperfeito do conjuntivo + condicional ('Se eu tivesse tempo, ia contigo'), the politeness uses ('Queria...', 'Se calhar era melhor que...') and 'como se' + conjuntivo; the classic English-speaker error is mapping 'If I had time' onto *'Se eu tinha tempo' because English uses a plain past — stress that hypothetical se never takes the imperfeito do indicativo — and point out that colloquial pt-PT normally prefers 'ia' to 'iria' in the main clause.

title: Future Subjunctive
blurbEn: You'll be able to talk about open future conditions — when you can, if you want, as soon as they arrive — the way every Portuguese speaker actually does.
notePrompt: Give this tense real weight: it is a living, everyday Portuguese tense with no English analogue and no Spanish equivalent in daily use, formed from the third person plural preterite stem so irregulars carry over intact (fizeram→fizer, foram→for, tiveram→tiver, puderam→puder, quiseram→quiser, disseram→disser), and it is obligatory after se, quando, enquanto, assim que, logo que, sempre que, conforme and depois de que whenever the event is still open; the anchor is 'quando puderes' / 'se quiseres' / 'assim que chegarem' against the systematic English-speaker error 'quando podes' / 'se queres', which comes straight from English using the present after 'when' and 'if' — and flag the trap that most futuro do conjuntivo forms are identical to the infinitivo pessoal (ser is where they split: for vs ser), so learners must know which structure they are inside.

title: Humour, Irony and Softening
blurbEn: You'll be able to disagree with a neighbour, query a bill and turn down an invitation without ever sounding blunt.
notePrompt: Teach the pt-PT softening toolkit — 'não é bem assim', 'se calhar', 'sabes como é', 'olha, não me leves a mal, mas...', 'estou a brincar', 'ora essa', 'até certo ponto' — together with understatement and the social ritual of queixar-se (complaining as bonding, not as a demand for action); the contrast to draw is the English 'I'm afraid I have to disagree' against the Portuguese move of opening in agreement and then reversing ('Pois, pois... agora lá que seja assim tão fácil, não é'), and the errors to correct are using 'desculpa' where 'com licença' is needed, delivering deadpan English sarcasm that reads as sincere rudeness, and mistaking Portuguese directness about bodies, age and money for aggression.

title: Work and Employment
blurbEn: You'll be able to read a Portuguese job advert, sit through a work meeting, and make sense of your own contract and payslip.
notePrompt: Cover the real paperwork and the real register: recibos verdes vs contrato a termo certo vs contrato sem termo, subsídio de férias and subsídio de Natal, Segurança Social, IRS retido na fonte, baixa médica, despedimento vs rescisão por mútuo acordo, plus currículo, carta de motivação and meeting language (dar seguimento, ficar com o dossiê, estar em cima do acontecimento); the contrast is pt-PT telemóvel de serviço, reunião, colega and ordenado against pt-BR celular, galera and salário-as-default, and the two English-speaker errors to name are *'aplicar para um emprego' for 'candidatar-se a um emprego' and *'suportar' for 'to support' where Portuguese wants 'apoiar'.

title: Compound Tenses: Indicative
blurbEn: You'll be able to say what has been going on lately and what had already happened before something else, without collapsing everything into the simple past.
notePrompt: Teach ter + particípio passado across the pretérito perfeito composto (tenho feito), the mais-que-perfeito composto (tinha feito), the futuro composto (terei feito) and the condicional composto (teria feito), noting that spoken pt-PT uses ter, never haver, and that 'tinha feito' has entirely displaced the synthetic 'fizera' outside literature; the make-or-break contrast is that 'tenho feito' is NOT the English present perfect — it means a repeated or continuing action across a recent stretch ('Tenho trabalhado muito' = I've been working a lot lately) — while a single completed event stays in the simple pretérito perfeito ('Já fiz isso'); the classic English-speaker error is *'Tenho tomado o pequeno-almoço' for 'I have had breakfast', which a Portuguese ear hears as a repeated habit.

title: Compound Tenses: Subjunctive
blurbEn: You'll be able to voice doubt and regret about things that already happened, including the whole 'if I had known' family.
notePrompt: Combine the conjuntivo of ter with the particípio: tenha feito for doubt about a completed event ('Espero que já tenham chegado'), tivesse feito for the unreal past ('Se eu tivesse sabido, tinha dito'), and tiver feito for a completed future condition ('Quando tiveres acabado, avisa-me'); the anchor contrast is the past-unreal conditional 'Se eu tivesse sabido, teria dito' against the two English-speaker errors *'Se eu tinha sabido' (English's plain past perfect after 'if') and 'Se eu soubesse' used for a past regret when soubesse is present-unreal — and note that colloquial pt-PT very often says 'tinha dito' where the grammar book prescribes 'teria dito'.

title: News and Current Affairs
blurbEn: You'll be able to follow the Telejornal and a talk-show panel talking over each other, and give your own take on a story at dinner.
notePrompt: Teach the register of Portuguese news — headline ellipsis and nominalisation ('Aprovada em Conselho de Ministros a subida das pensões'), the passive and the se-impersonal, the condicional de rumor ('teria admitido') — alongside the media landscape learners will meet: RTP1, SIC and TVI, the Telejornal, Público and Expresso, and the comentador panel format where everyone talks at once; contrast the compressed written headline with the spoken retelling learners actually need ('Ouvi dizer que...', 'Parece que...', 'Ao que consta...'), and address the false friends that make headlines misleading — 'atualmente' is currently not actually, 'eventualmente' is possibly not eventually, 'assistir a' is to watch not to help, and 'pretender' is to intend not to pretend.

title: Government and Politics
blurbEn: You'll be able to work out who actually decides what — from the junta de freguesia up to São Bento — and hold a political conversation without giving offence.
notePrompt: Map the real structures a resident deals with: freguesia and junta de freguesia → câmara municipal (presidente, vereadores) → distrito, then Assembleia da República and the Primeiro-Ministro at São Bento versus the Presidente da República at Belém, plus legislativas, autárquicas, círculo eleitoral, coligação, moção de censura and the party acronyms; the contrast to draw is Portugal's semi-presidential split against the English-speaker assumption of one head of government — the recurring error is calling the Primeiro-Ministro 'o Presidente' — and cover enough 25 de Abril and Estado Novo background to understand how older neighbours in the Oeste frame politics, plus the exits 'não estou muito por dentro' and 'lá isso não sei'.

title: Reported Speech: The Full Backshift
titlePt: O Discurso Indireto: A Concordância dos Tempos
blurbEn: You'll be able to pass on what someone else said — a message, an instruction, a piece of gossip — accurately and in one go.
notePrompt: B1 already introduced reporting present-tense speech; this is the DEEPENING pass, so open by referencing it. Teach the full concordância dos tempos: how each tense shifts when the reporting verb is in the past (presente→imperfeito, pretérito perfeito→mais-que-perfeito composto, futuro→condicional), plus the pronoun and deictic shifts (aqui→ali, hoje→nesse dia, este→esse). The English-speaker error is failing to backshift at all — «ele disse que está cansado» where pt-PT wants «ele disse que estava cansado».

title: Reported Speech in the Past
blurbEn: You'll be able to relay a whole conversation from yesterday, keeping every tense where a Portuguese ear expects to find it.
notePrompt: Drill the back-shift when the reporting verb is in the past: presente→imperfeito, pretérito perfeito→mais-que-perfeito composto (tinha feito), futuro→condicional, imperativo and presente do conjuntivo→imperfeito do conjuntivo, and futuro do conjuntivo→imperfeito do conjuntivo ('Quando puderes, liga-me' → 'Pediu-me que lhe ligasse quando pudesse'); the contrast to hammer is that English lets the tense stay put when the fact is still true ('He said he lives in Torres') while pt-PT back-shifts anyway ('Disse que morava em Torres'), and the English-speaker errors are leaving the present in place after a past reporting verb and reporting a command with an imperative instead of the imperfeito do conjuntivo.

title: Regional Accents and Dialects
blurbEn: You'll be able to understand the plumber from the Alentejo, the cousins from São Miguel and the neighbour who has never left the Oeste.
notePrompt: Work through the varieties this family will actually meet, with the specific sound substitutions rather than vague description: the local Estremadura/Oeste falar, close to the Lisbon standard but with heavier unstressed-vowel crushing and swallowed final syllables; Alentejano with its drawn-out vowels, 'ê' for 'ei' (fêjão, primêro) and a markedly commoner gerund ('estou fazendo') that contradicts the standard estar a + infinitivo; Algarvio, clipped and end-swallowing with an Andalusian-tinged rhythm; and Micaelense from São Miguel, where /u/ fronts towards a French-style ü (Lisboa → Lüsboa) and diphthongs shift, making it the hardest variety in the country for learners; the contrast to draw is Lisbon's crushed unstressed vowels against the fuller vowels of the north and the islands, and the error to correct is the learner who concludes their listening is bad — give them the substitution rules so they decode instead of guessing.

title: Carnival in Torres Vedras
blurbEn: You'll be able to follow the corso, get the jokes on the floats, and explain to a visitor why this is the most Portuguese carnival there is.
notePrompt: Give the real lexicon and the real culture of 'o mais português de Portugal': corso, carros alegóricos, matrafonas (men in women's clothes), cabeçudos, Zés-Pereiras, os Reis do Carnaval, entrudo, folião, and the satirical crítica social that is the whole point of the floats; the contrast to draw is Torres against the feathers-and-samba Rio carnival that Portuguese people will assume a foreigner has in mind — this one is mockery of politicians and local grievances, not spectacle — and the errors to address are reading 'fantasia' as fantasy when it means costume, and treating the political jokes as hostility rather than as licensed once-a-year mockery.

title: The Gerund, and Why Portugal Avoids It
titlePt: O Gerúndio e o «Estar a» + Infinitivo
blurbEn: You'll be able to use the gerund in the places European Portuguese genuinely wants it, and stop reaching for it everywhere English would.
notePrompt: Establish first that pt-PT expresses ongoing action with estar a + infinitivo ('Estou a comer') where pt-BR uses the gerund ('Estou comendo'), then teach where the gerund is genuinely alive in pt-PT: adverbial clauses of time, cause and manner ('Chegando a casa, telefono-te'; 'Sendo assim, fica para amanhã'; 'Tendo em conta o preço...'), the compound gerund ('Tendo acabado, saiu'), formal and written register, and its dialectal survival in the Alentejo and Algarve; the anchor contrast is 'Estou a trabalhar' vs the Brazilian 'Estou trabalhando', and the English-speaker error is mapping every '-ing' onto '-ndo' — *'Gosto de nadando' where Portuguese takes the plain infinitive (gosto de nadar), and *'Depois de comendo' where it takes 'depois de comer'.

title: Personal Infinitive vs Subjunctive
blurbEn: You'll be able to pick the lighter infinitive construction where a native speaker would, instead of grinding out a conjuntivo every single time.
notePrompt: Teach the inflected infinitive (fazer, fazeres, fazer, fazermos, fazerem) as the everyday alternative to the conjuntivo after prepositions, drilled as minimal pairs: 'para eu fazer' vs 'para que eu faça', 'antes de saíres' vs 'antes que saias', 'apesar de teres razão' vs 'embora tenhas razão', plus 'é melhor irmos', 'no caso de chegarmos tarde' and 'até eles voltarem'; the governing contrast is that a preposition takes the infinitivo pessoal while a conjunction built on 'que' takes the conjuntivo, and the two English-speaker errors are leaving the infinitive uninflected when the subject changes (*'para nós ir' for 'para nós irmos') and defaulting to the conjuntivo in slots where Portuguese finds it heavy — close by noting that many infinitivo pessoal forms are homographs of the futuro do conjuntivo, told apart only by what governs them.

title: The Lines of Torres Vedras
blurbEn: You'll be able to walk a visitor round the forts above your own town and follow a Portuguese guide narrating the Peninsular War at full speed.
notePrompt: Use the local Napoleonic fortifications as an extended listening-and-narrating unit: the Guerra Peninsular and the Invasões Francesas, Wellington's secret defensive lines built in 1809-10, the terra queimada policy that emptied the Oeste, the redutos and fortes at São Vicente, Zambujal and Alqueidão, and the Centro de Interpretação in Torres Vedras; the language focus is the narrative past working as a system — pretérito perfeito for events, imperfeito for background and habit, mais-que-perfeito composto for what had already happened — plus the historic present that guides use for drama; the English-speaker error to correct is telling the whole story in the pretérito perfeito because English gets by with one simple past, which flattens the narrative and turns scene-setting into a chain of events.

title: How the CIPLE Exam Works
blurbEn: You will be able to explain exactly what the three CIPLE components are, what each one is worth, what score you need, and where your twelve weeks of study should go.
notePrompt: Teach the shape of the exam before any Portuguese. CIPLE is the Certificado Inicial de Português Língua Estrangeira, the A2 exam of CAPLE at the Faculdade de Letras da Universidade de Lisboa; CAPLE's own FAQ calls A2 the minimum level for acquiring Portuguese nationality, and Portaria n.º 1403-A/2006, art. 1.º n.º 2, fixes A2 as 'conhecimento suficiente em língua portuguesa'. Three components are sat on one day: Compreensão da Leitura e Produção e Interação Escritas, 1h15, 45%; Compreensão do Oral, 30 minutes, 30%; Produção e Interação Orais, about 15 minutes for a PAIR of candidates, 25% — roughly two hours in total plus a 15-minute break. The pass is 55% of the weighted total (0,45 x leitura/escrita + 0,30 x compreensão do oral + 0,25 x produção oral); the bands are Suficiente 55-69%, Bom 70-84%, Muito Bom 85-100%, and below 55% CAPLE's FAQ uses the label Insuficiente and issues a Comunicação de Resultados instead of a certificate. Say honestly that CAPLE publishes NO minimum per component — preparation sites claim 25% or 45%, they contradict each other and none of them cites CAPLE — so the safe rule is to aim for 55% in every component and never plan to sacrifice one. Do the weighting arithmetic out loud: reading plus writing is almost half the exam and is the most trainable part for an adult who already lives in Portugal, so it earns the most hours. Give the shape of the twelve weeks: week 0 secure the exam seat, weeks 1-2 diagnose and rebuild the A2 spine, weeks 3-7 reading and writing, weeks 6-9 listening, weeks 8-11 the paired oral, week 12 full timed mocks. Warn once, inventing nothing: since 19 May 2026 nationality also requires knowledge of culture, history, national symbols (Lei Orgânica n.º 1/2026, art. 6.º n.º 1 al. c) and of rights, duties and political organisation (al. d); nationals of Portuguese-speaking countries are presumed to satisfy only the LANGUAGE part of c); and as of August 2026 the implementing regulation for that civics test had not been published, so its format, price and dates are unknown and must never be stated. Mention that a school version, CIPLE-e, exists for ages 12-15.

title: The Cold Diagnostic
blurbEn: You will be able to sit CAPLE's published model papers under the real clock, score yourself with the real weighting, and name the component that is costing you the pass.
notePrompt: This unit is a procedure, not a lesson: the learner gets a real baseline in week 1, before studying anything. CAPLE publishes a free model set — the reading and writing paper (6 pages), the listening paper (4 pages), a 30-minute audio file and a single answer key covering both papers; there is NO published model for the oral component, so that one is rehearsed with a partner instead. Instruct them to sit the written paper with a pencil, a blue or black pen and a 75-minute timer, take a 15-minute break, then play the listening audio from start to finish without pausing: the audio is exactly thirty minutes long and IS the component, so there is no reading time before it and no extra time after it. Scoring: 20 reading items plus 2 written texts in the first paper, 25 items in the listening; turn each component into a percentage, then compute the weighted total 0,45 / 0,30 / 0,25 and compare it with 55%. Give the landmarks but flag the assumption: about 14 of 25 listening items is roughly 55% of that component and about 18 of 25 is roughly 70%, on the assumption of equal item weighting, which CAPLE does not publish. Make them write down three numbers, one per component, and the two worst task types by name, because everything after this unit is triage. Be honest that the two written texts cannot be self-scored objectively — CAPLE publishes no marking grid for them — so judge them only against what the paper itself demands: the word count, the addressee and every instruction in the prompt. Tell them to repeat the whole run in week 12, and to do the listening after 75 minutes of written work rather than fresh, because that is the real condition on the day.

title: Counters and Services: the Ten Places
titlePt: Balcões e Serviços: Os Dez Espaços
blurbEn: You will be able to tell, from a single overheard sentence, which counter or public service you are standing at — and say the five phrases you need there.
notePrompt: Build this unit on the ten espaços de comunicação that CAPLE's own listening paper uses in Parte 2, because that list is published and verbatim: escola, táxi, mercado, centro de saúde, agência de emprego, consulado/embaixada, restaurante, correios, aeroporto, loja de produtos informáticos. For each place teach the five things you would hear ONLY there — correios: selo, carta registada, encomenda, levantar, código postal; centro de saúde: marcar uma consulta, receita, tenho dores, número de utente, análises; agência de emprego: candidatura, currículo, entrevista, contrato, a tempo inteiro; consulado ou embaixada: visto, autorização de residência, senha, impresso, passaporte; aeroporto: embarque, bagagem de mão, porta, atraso, cartão de embarque; táxi: leve-me a…, pode parar aqui, o troco, praça de táxis; mercado: um quilo de, quanto é o quilo?, está fresco?, mais alguma coisa?; restaurante: a ementa, o prato do dia, a conta, uma bica; escola: a aula, o horário, os trabalhos de casa, a inscrição; loja de informática: garantia, carregador, ecrã, avariado, talão. Flag the counter words that decide whole exam items: senha is the numbered queue ticket and not a password, impresso is a form to fill in, visto is a visa, talão de compra is the receipt, trocar and devolver are what you do with a faulty purchase, renda and arrendar belong to housing. Teach the transaction frame as one block, since it is reused in the oral role-play: 'Bom dia. Queria…, se faz favor', 'Quanto é?', 'Pode ajudar-me?', 'Onde é que fica…?', 'Tenho de trazer mais alguma coisa?', 'Posso trocar isto?'. Point out how immigrant-shaped the official list is — agência de emprego, consulado, centro de saúde — and that this same vocabulary reappears in the reading notices and in the oral simulation, so it is paid for three times. Insist on the European forms throughout: autocarro, comboio, paragem, telemóvel, casa de banho, pequeno-almoço, empregado de mesa, sumo, ementa, frigorífico, talho, multibanco, morada, apelido. Drill it as 'o que se diz onde': give one sentence and ask for the place, then reverse it and ask for a sentence that could only be said there.

title: Notices, Timetables and Small Ads
blurbEn: You will be able to read a Portuguese public notice or classified ad at speed and answer the one question that turns on a single word.
notePrompt: This is pure exam lexicon and it is the highest-yield vocabulary in the whole CIPLE, because five reading items are built directly on it and the same words come back in the listening. Teach the notice set as a closed list: dias úteis, horário de atendimento, horário contínuo, encerra, encerrado, feriados, marcação prévia, visitas guiadas, preço especial, prazo, a partir de, até, destinatários, local, documentos necessários, avariado, proibido, obras, aviso, senha. Then the classified-ad set: arrenda-se (the Portuguese verb — aluga-se is Brazilian), T2, mobilado, varanda, zona comercial, renda, oferece-se, procuro trabalho, televendas, carta de condução de ligeiros, carro próprio, currículo, em anexo. The genres attested on CAPLE's own paper are an apartment ad, an opening-hours notice for the Serviços de Identificação Civil, a museum notice, a job ad and a school-enrolment notice laid out under DESTINATÁRIOS, PRAZO, LOCAL and DOCUMENTOS NECESSÁRIOS (cartão de cidadão e boletim de vacinas) — reproduce that shape when you write practice items. Make the two mechanical skills explicit, because both appear: comparing two rows of the same timetable (Lisboa das 8h30 às 19h30 contra Porto das 9h00 às 16h00) and converting a condition into a true-or-false claim (todas as crianças nascidas no ano de 2007). Teach the trap the real model contains: an ad headed EMPREGO: OFERECE-SE whose body reads 'Procuro trabalho na área de televendas' — the writer wants work, and a candidate who answers from the heading instead of the text loses the item. Add the institutional nouns that also serve the nationality process: Cartão de Cidadão, boletim de vacinas, Serviços de Identificação Civil, Centro de Emprego, junta de freguesia, atestado de residência, comprovativo de morada. Drill by handing over a notice plus one three-option question and requiring the learner to point at the exact words that make each option true or false; if they cannot find the words, it is not the answer.

title: Numbers, Times, Prices and Directions
blurbEn: You will be able to catch a time, a price, a floor and a turning first time, at Portuguese speed, and write them down without a replay.
notePrompt: Sell this unit as the cheapest marks in the exam: whole listening items are decided by two seconds of audio — 14h30 against 18h30, or '1.º andar, 2.ª porta à direita' against 'à esquerda'. Teach the European numerals explicitly against the Brazilian ones most learners arrive with: catorze (not quatorze), dezasseis, dezassete, dezanove (not dezesseis, dezessete, dezenove). Cover the clock both ways, because the exam uses both: às seis e meia, às seis e um quarto, um quarto para as sete, dezoito e trinta, meio-dia, meia-noite, da manhã, da tarde, da noite. Teach the time expressions that carry rules rather than just times: quinze dias means a fortnight, daqui a uma semana, na semana seguinte à compra, dias úteis, ao fim de semana, dentro de uma hora, há dois anos for elapsed time. Money next: quanto é?, quanto custa?, dois euros e cinquenta, vinte e cinco euros, o troco, o talão, multibanco, levantar dinheiro, pagar a pronto. Directions and position are a guaranteed topic in both the listening and the oral: rés-do-chão, primeiro andar, segundo andar, à direita, à esquerda, em frente, ao lado de, ao fundo de, no meio de, por baixo de, por cima de, em frente de, junto a, no fim das escadas, vire à direita, siga em frente, atravesse a rua, apanhe o autocarro na paragem. Anchor the whole lot on two verbs that make these answerable in speech: ficar for location ('a farmácia fica ao lado do hotel') and haver ('há um multibanco ao fundo da rua'). Prescribe the drill and say why it works: five minutes a day of ten spoken numbers, times, prices and floor-plus-side directions, written down with no replay — dictation exposes exactly what a feeling of 'understanding' hides.

title: The House, the Furniture and the Professions
titlePt: A Casa, a Mobília e as Profissões
blurbEn: You will be able to describe a photograph of a room or a family for two minutes, and say which job you would like and why.
notePrompt: This unit exists because of one repeatedly reported fact: furniture and the rooms of a house are the vocabulary that catches CIPLE candidates out, since the oral has been reported to hand each candidate a different photograph to describe for about two minutes — an empty kitchen, a furnished room, a family dining in a restaurant. Teach the divisions of the house (sala, cozinha, quarto, casa de banho, corredor, varanda, garagem, sótão, cave) with the furniture and appliances (sofá, poltrona, mesa, cadeira, armário, estante, cómoda, cama, mesa de cabeceira, candeeiro, tapete, cortinas, frigorífico, fogão, forno, micro-ondas, máquina de lavar a loiça). Insist on the European items as you go: frigorífico not geladeira, casa de banho not banheiro, ecrã not tela, telemóvel not celular. Bolt the prepositions of place straight onto the nouns, because a description is nouns plus positions and nothing else: 'à esquerda está o frigorífico', 'à direita está o fogão', 'no meio há uma mesa de madeira com quatro cadeiras', 'o sofá está ao lado da janela', 'por cima da mesa há um candeeiro'. Give a description skeleton to memorise and reuse for any image: 'Nesta fotografia vejo…', then left/right/middle, then what people are doing — always estar a + infinitivo, so 'estão a jantar' and 'estão a conversar', never the Brazilian gerund — then 'Parecem contentes' and 'Acho que é…'. Then teach professions, because a published task hands the pair a sheet of five (polícia, bombeiro, professor, taxista, enfermeiro) and asks which they would choose: add médico, cozinheiro, empregado de mesa, motorista, canalizador, eletricista, agricultor, informático, reformado, desempregado. Drill the opinion frame in the imperfeito de cortesia, which is the A2 politeness workhorse: 'Gostava de ser enfermeira, porque gosto de ajudar as pessoas' and 'Não gostava de ser polícia, porque é um trabalho perigoso e as horas são difíceis'.

title: The A2 Grammar Spine
blurbEn: You will be able to run the whole A2 grammar checklist and say, for each item, whether you can produce it or only recognise it.
notePrompt: Open by saying plainly that CAPLE publishes no official programa, no grammar list and no wordlist for the CIPLE: this checklist is reconstructed from the Referencial Camões PLE (2017), the QECR A2 descriptors and, above all, from what CAPLE's own sample papers actually contain. Verbs are the level itself: presente do indicativo, regular and irregular; pretérito perfeito simples as the narrative workhorse (cheguei, apanhei, disseram, teve, ficou, resolveram); pretérito imperfeito for background and description (estava, tinha, era, podia); and the imperfeito de cortesia taught as a politeness formula before it is taught as a tense — 'Queria um café, se faz favor', 'Gostava de trabalhar aqui'. Drill the perífrases as single units, because they carry more A2 meaning than any conjugation table: ir + infinitivo for the future (vou ler, vamos ver), estar a + infinitivo for the progressive — 'estou a falar', NEVER 'estou falando', which is Brazilian and reads as a register failure — plus ter de + infinitivo for obligation, acabar de, começar a, continuar a and conseguir + infinitivo. Teach 'há' for elapsed time, because it appears in the oral every single time: 'Vivo em Portugal há três anos', 'Estudo português há dois anos', 'Ficou desempregada há seis meses'. Clitic placement is a first-class A2 topic in Portugal: enclisis by default in affirmative main clauses (chamo-me, dá-me, disseram-lhes, avariou-se) and proclisis after negation, after 'que' and after certain adverbs (não me telefones, que te enviei, já se foi embora); the classic stumble is telefona-me turning into não me telefones. Add the written traps attested on the paper: 'Já chegámos' with the acute accent that marks the past in Portugal, and the Acordo Ortográfico spellings as applied here — ativa, eletrónica, aspeto, but contacto and facto keep their c. Drill the rubric imperatives as exam-survival vocabulary, since a candidate who cannot decode them cannot sit the paper: Leia, Escreva, Faça, Responda, Identifique, Escolha, Marque, Use. Close on connectors, because two linked simple sentences beat one ambitious broken one at A2: porque, mas, e, depois, também, por isso, quando, além disso, uma vez que.

title: Reading: The Four Tasks
titlePt: Compreensão da Leitura: As Quatro Tarefas
blurbEn: You will be able to recognise all four reading tasks on sight and attack each one with the right technique instead of reading everything twice.
notePrompt: Parte 1 of the 75-minute paper is exactly 20 items in four tasks of five, all marked in pencil on the folha de respostas. Tarefa A, questions 1-5: a one-line situation is matched to one of three SMS-style telemóvel messages; every distractor is a plausible message about the same topic, so what really decides it is who is speaking, to whom, and when — already arrived against still travelling, asking against thanking. Tarefa B, questions 6-10: five short authentic notices and ads, one three-option question each (an apartment ad, a public-service opening-hours notice, a museum notice, a job ad, a school enrolment notice); answer from the words on the page and never from world knowledge, because the published model contains an ad headed EMPREGO: OFERECE-SE whose correct answer is that the writer is looking for work. Tarefa C, questions 11-15: a matching task over a formal carta de candidatura a emprego — five sentence stems in coluna A against EIGHT options in coluna B, each usable once, so exactly three are never used; teach elimination, cross options off as they are committed, and check that precisely three are left over, because the distractors are deliberate mirrors ('os pais ainda não estavam cá' against 'os pais já cá viviam há alguns anos'). Tarefa D, questions 16-20: one longer narrative or journalistic text of roughly 300 words with five three-option questions that follow the order of the text; in the model they turn on cause and motive rather than bare facts, and on reported speech ('disseram-lhes que…'). Teach one universal technique for all four: for every option, put a finger on the words in the text that make it true or false — if you cannot find them, it is not the answer. Nothing in CAPLE's model, key or Normas mentions negative marking, so never leave an item blank; with three options a guess is worth a third of a mark and costs nothing anyone can find. Mention honestly that CAPLE's older published specification also lists verdadeiro/falso items, which do not appear in the current model — spend ten minutes on them so they cannot surprise anyone, and no more.

title: Writing: The Two Texts
blurbEn: You will be able to produce both CIPLE written texts to length, in the right register, from a skeleton you can write out from memory.
notePrompt: Parte 2 of the written paper is two texts and nothing else, and they are very different tasks. Texto 1 is written INTERACTION of 25-35 words: the model has friends texting 'Já chegámos. Estamos à tua espera no café do parque. Ainda demoras?', so the reply must actually answer the direct question with a time; the instruction reads 'deve ter uma extensão de 25-35 palavras', with no 'cerca de', so treat that range as exact. Texto 2 is written PRODUCTION of about 60-80 words: an informal email to friends whose opening line is supplied — 'Caros Amigos, Queria muito estar convosco no fim de semana, mas não consegui' — and the task is to narrate what went wrong, which forces pretérito perfeito simples for the events plus 'estava a + infinitivo' for the background. Both texts go to friends in the PLURAL, so the forms are vocês, o vosso, convosco, esperem, desculpem; warn that the exam's own instructions address the candidate as 'Você marcou um encontro…' and that mirroring 'você' back into a message to friends is wrong-footed in Portugal. Give two skeletons to memorise: Texto 1 — apologise, give the reason, give the time, close ('Olá! Desculpem o atraso. Perdi o autocarro e estou à espera do próximo. Estou a chegar daqui a vinte minutos. Até já!'); Texto 2 — apologise, narrate two or three things in order, close forward-looking ('Na sexta-feira à noite, o carro avariou-se… No sábado, a minha filha ficou doente… Peço imensa desculpa. Espero que possamos combinar outro fim de semana em breve. Um abraço,'). Three mechanical rules void otherwise perfect Portuguese: the texts must be on the folha de respostas in blue or black pen, since answers in pencil or left on the rascunho are not marked at all; the candidate may never write their real name anywhere on the exam, which annuls it, so choose one invented signing name and always practise with it; and the supplied opening of Texto 2 is a stimulus, not word count, so write 60-80 words of your own. Teach word-count control physically — learn what 30 and 70 words look like in your own handwriting, count one full line and multiply, and do it once at the end, not while writing. Be honest that CAPLE publishes no marking grid for these texts, so the only certain criteria are the instructions printed on the paper: word count, task, addressee — and the safe style is short, clear, correct sentences joined with porque, mas, depois, também and por isso, not ambitious ones that multiply errors.

title: Managing the 75-Minute Paper
blurbEn: You will be able to walk into the biggest paper with a minute-by-minute plan, so that the reading never eats your writing.
notePrompt: The structural flaw of this paper is that 20 reading items sit in front of the two written texts with no bell between them, so the commonest way to lose 45% of the exam is to write Texto 2 in the last six minutes, or not at all. Give the plan and make the learner rehearse it under a timer at least three times: minutes 0-2, check the folha de respostas, the pencil, the eraser and the blue or black pen; 2-9, questions 1-5; 9-20, questions 6-10; 20-31, questions 11-15; 31-43, questions 16-20; a HARD STOP at minute 43 to verify every pencil mark and fill every blank with a guess; 46-56, Texto 1; 56-71, Texto 2 with roughly three minutes planning, nine writing and three checking; 71-75, count the words of both texts and sweep. Teach the physical switch as a ritual: put the pencil down and pick the pen up before Texto 1, because candidates who carry the pencil across from Parte 1 write an unmarkable text. Offer the legitimate alternative for anyone who panics about time — write Parte 2 first while fresh, then do the reading tired — and say clearly that the point is having a plan, not which of the two you pick. The final sweep is targeted, not a re-read: agreement of gender and number, then verb endings, then accents, then legibility, in that order, because ambiguous handwriting is simply read as an error. Remind them that candidates may not leave the room before the scheduled end, so there is never a reason to stop checking. Set the practice protocol: three timed runs of the whole paper, at least one on real paper with a real pen rather than a screen, scored on one question only — did the plan hold, and was Texto 2 finished with time to check it?

title: Listening: 25 Items in 30 Minutes
titlePt: Compreensão do Oral: 25 Questões em 30 Minutos
blurbEn: You will be able to work the listening paper the way it is actually built — pre-reading fast, marking as you go, and transferring 25 answers without a slip.
